items.title: Close race as Iceland votes on whether to restart talks on joining EU
items.summary: Turbulent international affairs have brought the vote forward, but the campaign has focused more on Iceland's vital fishing industry.
items.content:
Icelanders are voting in a referendum to decide whether to resume talks on joining the European Union, 13 years after they were broken off.

In an indication of how tight the result is expected to be, the latest opinion poll put the No campaign in the lead with 51.6%. An earlier poll had put the Yes campaign ahead.

Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir's centre-left government had already intended to hold a referendum, but turbulent international affairs prompted her to bring it forward.

But the debate was fought less over Nato member Iceland's security concerns than over its vital fishing industry and sovereignty.

Voting is due to go on from 09:00 to 22:00 GMT on Saturday and the result is expected in the early hours of Sunday.

Iceland has a population of under 400,000. More than one in five voters had already cast their ballots in early voting before Saturday, according to Iceland's public broadcaster RUV.

The question on the ballot is , external : "Should Iceland resume accession negotiations with the European Union?"

Although Iceland is already part of the EU's single market and Schengen border-free zone as part of the European Economic Area, EU membership would bring it into the customs union and eventually the euro.

Iceland's application to join the EU was already well advanced when it put talks on hold in 2013, and European Commission officials have indicated that talks could be finalised in one or two years. Of the 35 so-called chapters of talks ranging from fisheries and economic policy to freedom of speech and free movement of goods, 27 had begun and 11 of them were provisionally complete , external .

A Yes vote would not be a final decision on joining the EU. It would mean backing a move towards an accession agreement. Any deal would then have to be approved by a second referendum, as well by parliament, and the constitution would have to be amended. The EU's 27 member states would also have to sign it off.

One Yes-campaign group, "Yes to See", says Icelanders should at least see what deal they can get, so they have all the information before a final decision.

Equally, a No vote would not rule out the chance of Iceland resuming talks in the future.

Read more: Iceland knife-edge vote that could be decided on fish

Sovereignty has been a crucial issue in the pre-referendum debate. Iceland fought hard to become fully independent from Denmark in 1944, and its fishing and marine industries make up almost 40% of exports.

The No campaign fears losing control over Iceland's prized fishing grounds under the EU's Common Fisheries Policy and has vowed never to share the country's waters with anyone. Brussels has indicated Iceland could earn some kind of exemption, but it is considered potentially the biggest obstacle to any agreement.

Many Icelanders remember the so-called Cod Wars with the UK that Iceland won in the 1970s. And fisheries was always the issue that stopped Iceland joining the EU before.

However, in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis and the collapse of Iceland's banking system, Reykjavik moved to start accession talks in 2009, only to bring them to a halt in 2013.

Iceland is now one of Europe's most affluent nations and Eirikur Bergmann, professor of politics at Bifröst University, told the BBC that "many people attribute this to Iceland's independence".

One Icelandic trade union survey suggested this year that the country was the most expensive in the world, far pricier than its Nordic neighbours.

Although it has the fifth highest GDP (economic output) per capita in the world, interest rates are stubbornly high at 8% and inflation has climbed to 5.6%.

Yes campaigners argue that the economic benefits of the EU would help bring the rates down.

Iceland may be a founder member of Nato but it has no military and relies on its allies for defence.

A bilateral US defence agreement has been in place since 1951 and the No campaign has said Iceland's security rests on both Nato and the US, and that EU membership is not a substitute for Nato.

Iceland has been a strong supporter of Ukraine during Russia's full-scale invasion and officials have viewed Russia's increased maritime manoeuvres near the island with alarm.

However, there has also been concern at US President Donald Trump's expressed interest in taking over Greenland - especially the fact that he has confused it with Iceland.

This year the EU and Iceland signed a security and defence partnership, and EU officials said the EU "offers an anchor in a community of values, prosperity and security".

Ahead of the referendum, the two sides held a televised debate where the Yes campaign team was headed by Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir and the No campaign was led by Guðrún Hafsteinsdóttir, chair of the opposition Independence Party.

Kristrún told the audience that Iceland was already well integrated in the European Union, and becoming a member would be "one of the biggest risk-reducing steps we can take".

She also made clear that a Yes vote did not necessarily mean that Iceland would join, and that if there was a No vote, the result would be respected.

Guðrún, meanwhile, stressed that the vote was not about whether Iceland should work well with Europe: "We already do, and we want that to continue."

Instead, she portrayed the referendum as a vote on whether Icelanders wanted to hand "decision-making powers" to Brussels on fisheries, agriculture and their natural resources.

Although geopolitics kick-started the government's decision to push for a return to EU talks, there has been little discussion of it during the campaign.

"It's lower on the agenda than many would think," says Hallgrimur Oddsson, director of EU-Iceland think-tank European Currents.

items.title: Dolly Parton's dad couldn't read - it inspired her to send books to millions of children
items.summary: Families across the globe share how free books from Parton's Imagination Library helped their children.
items.content:
Across the globe in Australia, a toddler with speech delays delighted her family with her first word - "orange" - after she and her twin sister received a free book in the post about colours. It came from Imagination Library, the literacy programme begun by late global superstar Dolly Parton.

Parton, who died this week aged 80, launched the philanthropic effort in 1995 to honour her father - whose difficult Appalachian upbringing never allowed him to finish school or learn to read and write.

"He was the smartest man I have ever known, but I know in my heart his inability to read probably kept him from fulfilling all of his dreams," wrote Parton in an open letter on Imagination Library's website.

Imagination Library sends one free book a month to children from birth to age five. It first launched in Tennessee's Sevier County, where Parton grew up, before expanding across the US in 2000. The programme, which partners with local organisations, launched in Canada in 2006, the UK the following year, then Australia in 2013 and Ireland in 2019.

By 2025, as Imagination Library celebrated its 30th anniversary, it had distributed more than 300m books - equating to one book mailed every 78 seconds, according to the organisation.

And for the families in receipt of the storybooks, the impact has been invaluable.

Tennessee governor plans to name Nashville airport after Dolly Parton

"It just blows my mind that it's readily available for every family that lives in my borough," said London mother-of-two Harriet Anscombe, whose four-year-old daughter has been receiving Imagination Library books since she was three months old.

The free books helped Anscombe establish a reading-focused nighttime routine.

"I think that, if I didn't get those books, maybe I wouldn't have started doing bedtime stories till she was two - but because we were getting them so early, it embedded story time into our routine from when she was just a couple of months old," Anscombe said. "She probably doesn't remember a time when we weren't reading stories."

Imagination Library became part of the family routine for Ciara Fernandez Faber, too, after she signed up her son about eight years ago in Colorado. His favourite book for years was one written by Parton herself: I Am A Rainbow.

"We read it almost every night, and I never got tired of reading it to him," said Faber, 42.

"It's a book about different emotions, and so we would act out the different emotions, the different faces," she said. "At the back of the book, there's a little excerpt by Dolly talking about how everybody has a rainbow of feelings, and we would read that - and he would always point to her picture and say, 'There's the Book Queen.'"

Families like Faber's repeatedly remarked on how well curated the books were - detailing how topics helped their children not just with reading, but also with social and emotional development.

"There were themes that were addressed in a lot of the books that would have really helped us navigate issues," said Helen Cashell, of Dublin, Ireland.

She signed up both of her children, now aged seven and five, for the scheme. "Whether it was same-sex families or just different types of families, things about bravery, courage, bullying, things about different identities."

Author Selina Brown, whose book My Rice Is Best was selected for distribution through Imagination Library, noted how the plotline features a black protagonist.

The programme also helps promote authors like herself; because of the selection, it "means 14,000 copies of my book have been sent to children in the UK".

"To choose between gas, electric, food or a book, you're going to choose a core need - but with the Dolly Parton Imagination Library, you don't have to do that," she said.

In inner-city Sydney, Australia, first-time mum Paige Stewart was astounded as she watched her children's progress with the programme.

Her twin girls, now four, "had a speech delay and some learning difficulties" - but Stewart noticed a change after just the second book.

"Not only did they learn their colours from that book… it kind of set the tone for them speaking and their joy for books."

She's become a vocal advocate for the programme, telling others: "It's so helpful, honestly."

Alabama grandmother Kristina Hadley also promotes the programme to friends and family - even incorporating Imagination Library into baby gifts.

"I'll pull up the Imagination books website, and I'll print that, and I'll put it in a picture frame, and I'll get little newborn books and stuff like that, and I'll put it with that for like a suggestion for new mothers," said Hadley, 53.

She signed up her nearly three-year-old granddaughter, Eillie Elaine, "before she was actually born". Now the child has her own bookshelf in their shared household - "and one whole shelf is for her Dolly books".

"She likes to go to go to the mailbox, and she's like, 'Ms Dolly! Ms Dolly!' and I'm like, 'Well, let's go see if Ms Dolly sent you a book!'"

A lifelong Parton fan, Hadley chokes up while detailing how she was at work when a friend texted to say the singer had died.

Imagination Library, she says, "is going to keep her memory going with the younger generation, and I hope and I pray that this is something that goes on for years and years and years."

It's a legacy that Parton built quietly in the background as she presided over pop culture for more than six decades.

"The biggest thing that I like is the fact that she didn't do anything for recognition," said Geoff Blacklin, 67, of Manitoba, Canada.

He and his wife signed up their grandchildren for Imagination Library after a local doctor brought the programme to their region.

"She gave families more than books," Blacklin said. "She gave children a love of reading, precious moments with loved ones, and opportunities to learn and dream."

Such family stories and gratitude would undoubtedly have been music to Parton's ears; the expansion of the programme was truly a realisation of her own dream.

"In the beginning, my hope was simply to inspire the children in my home county, but here we are today with a worldwide programme that gives a book a month to well over 3 million children," she wrote on the Imagination Library site - also taking care to thank the partners "who have embraced my dream and made it their own".

At the centre of it, always, was her love for children - and her love for her father.

"Before he passed away, my Daddy told me the Imagination Library was probably the most important thing I had ever done," Parton wrote.

"I can't tell you how much that meant to me, because I created the Imagination Library as a tribute to my Daddy."

Dolly Parton was the one thing most Americans could agree on

Heart, hope and a steely determination: Dolly Parton's musical legacy

'Angel by my side' - Miley Cyrus pays tribute to godmother Dolly Parton

items.title: Landlady to 9/11 hijackers reveals their links to alleged Saudi spy
items.summary: A woman who rented out homes to two al-Qaeda members speaks publicly for the first time - to the BBC.
items.content:
Holly Ratchford still cannot believe that the man who moved into the residential complex she once managed would go on to be accused of involvement in the darkest day in recent US history.

"It's almost impossible for me to wrap my head around who he said he was, and who he really is. I still struggle with that," she tells the BBC.

The man, Omar al-Bayoumi - a Saudi in his early 40s - moved to the complex in San Diego, California, with his family in September 1999.

The new resident at number 152 Parkwood Apartments quickly became a regular at Ratchford's pool parties. "He was always so bubbly and smiling," she recalls, "and just very, very friendly."

A few months later, Bayoumi would introduce Ratchford to two apparently unassuming, "polite" men, who would also become her neighbours.

The pair would become infamous for hijacking American Airlines flight 77, and crashing it into the Pentagon, in the 9/11 attacks.

Ratchford has been haunted by her connection to these three men for the past 25 years. She feels she was taken in by Bayoumi from the start.

"Whenever I had parties he would come and be a part of the activities," she recalls, adding that his family would invite her in for food.

But Bayoumi, the one-time resident of 152 Parkwood, is now at the centre of the $1 trillion (£733bn) lawsuit brought against the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia by several thousand families of victims and as well as survivors of 9/11.

On 11 September 2001, four passenger aircraft were hijacked by 19 members of the Islamist extremist network, al-Qaeda. In addition to the crash at the Pentagon - the US military's headquarters near Washington DC - two planes were flown into the twin towers of the World Trade Center in New York, causing both buildings to collapse. A fourth crashed in a field in Pennsylvania, following resistance from passengers on board.

In all, almost 3,000 people were killed, including about 300 firefighters and other emergency workers at the World Trade Center.

Bayoumi is alleged to have facilitated the 9/11 plot through the support he provided for the first two hijackers to arrive in the US - Nawaf al-Hazmi and Khalid al-Mihdhar - who lived at Parkwood for several months prior to the attacks.

The federal judge in the 9/11 families' lawsuit in New York found a year ago that the evidence created "a reasonable inference" that Bayoumi and a Saudi diplomat based in the US had been "co-ordinating with the Saudi government when providing assistance to the hijackers".

The judge's ruling has allowed the families' case to move forward. Saudi Arabia is appealing it and, together with Bayoumi, has always denied the allegations.

Ever since the attacks, Bayoumi has been the subject of reporting and speculation.

Ratchford - who saw him interacting with the hijackers and witnessed him providing a crucial act of support for them - has given a sealed declaration to the New York court.

After unwittingly becoming embroiled in the investigation into what the US government has described as "the most egregious criminal act on American soil in modern history", she moved about as far from humanity as you can get in the United States.

I tracked her down to the high desert in the western US - rattlesnake country. She told me she avoided the news, and definitely did not speak to journalists. But, to my surprise, she agreed to talk.

Her interview with me casts doubt on the version of events Bayoumi has told police, the FBI and the New York court, and features in the BBC Radio 4 podcast, Intrigue: A 9/11 Story , and an upcoming BBC Panorama, 9/11: The Saudi Connection .

Twenty-five years on from the deadliest terror attack in history, Jane McMullen asks why thousands of grieving families are still fighting for answers.

In early 1999, Ratchford landed on her feet. Life before then had been untethered - she had moved around, been married, pregnant and divorced before she was 21. But now, aged 27, she had a job she loved and a home.

As the new property manager of Parkwood Apartments, a squat complex of 175 low-rise apartments and townhouses in the San Diego suburbs, she says she excelled. Properties were never empty for long. But it was not the paperwork, nor the healthy pay check, that made the job a dream, it was the people.

Ratchford not only worked at Parkwood, she lived there too. Her clients were also her neighbours. And many were more than that - she says they became her friends.

"I always told my staff: 'You make them feel like this is their home, and they'll stay,'" she recalls.

As Ratchford made her mark at Parkwood, she was happy and secure in the world she had built - a world in which she knew everyone and everything.

Omar al-Bayoumi moved into Parkwood claiming to be a mature student.

"I knew he was going to school. I'm not sure, other than that, what he did," Ratchford says.

More than two decades later, declassified FBI documents and court filings would reveal that Bayoumi's studies had, in effect, come to a halt in 1998. He was spending much more time organising religious activities in the Muslim community, which he often videotaped.

His constant filming, and his inquiring questions, aroused suspicions.

"It was a general consensus of people in the San Diego Muslim community that Bayoumi was an operative of the Saudi intelligence service," Richard Lambert, who led the city's FBI office investigation after 9/11, tells me.

But it was not Ratchford's business to pry. What mattered to her was whether he could pay the rent. And he could.

The FBI would later discover he was being paid about $90,000 (£55,600 at the time) a year.

The Bayoumi who Ratchford saw was captured on his never-before-broadcast home movies - throwing a ball around with his family by the Parkwood pool, laughing when it drifted into the water.

Another video reveals him on an excursion to Las Vegas with his family. Wearing a floral shirt, he points out the rollercoaster by the New York, New York hotel casino.

"I bought into everything that he told me. I really thought that's how he was," Ratchford says.

But that version of Bayoumi is at odds with the man who emerges from other videos.

In summer 1999, Bayoumi filmed the United States Capitol in Washington DC from different angles, noting a "plan", and turning the camera on himself to deliver a reporter-style commentary.

The 9/11 families' lawyers allege he was surveilling the building as a potential target for the attacks. The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia maintains it is a tourist video.

In his August 2025 judgement, the New York judge found that "all the Court can conclude" from the video is that Bayoumi "visited Washington DC and that he filmed the city".

On 3 February 2000, Bayoumi brought two young men into Ratchford's San Diego rental office. In an obvious hurry, she says, he perched on the filing cabinet as he told her that the two men were from his mosque and were staying with him while they looked for a place to rent.

"There was absolutely nothing unusual about them. They were nice, they were polite," she recalls.

The two men spoke no English, but Bayoumi took charge. Ratchford says he asked her what the two men would need to show in order to qualify for a Parkwood apartment.

"They didn't meet the income criteria at all, or the bank account. They had none of that," she tells me.

But the two men did have several thousand dollars in cash. Bank records show that, the following day, Bayoumi took them to the nearest bank and helped them open an account.

Back at Ratchford's office on the third day, he figured a way around the problematic income criterion. He would co-sign their lease - becoming the legal guarantor for their apartment.

The rental agreement shows Bayoumi's multiple signatures. He was their guarantor, their friend, their emergency contact, and his Parkwood home was listed as their current address.

Without further delay, the two men moved into number 150, a one-bed apartment just a few doors down from Bayoumi's poolside townhouse.

The two men Bayoumi was assuming legal responsibility for - Nawaf al-Hazmi and Khalid al-Mihdhar - would become 9/11 hijackers.

Hazmi and Mihdhar stayed in their apartment until the end of May that year, and then moved out. Ratchford thought no more about it.

Sixteen months later, as America reeled in shock and grief in the days following the 9/11 attacks, she says a woman called asking her for a rental reference for them. Without thinking, she rattled off their details.

But the woman was not a property agent - she was a reporter.

Her next question shook Ratchford: "Did you know that they were two of the terrorists that flew their plane into the Pentagon?"

On 14 September 2001, two special agents interviewed Ratchford in her Parkwood office.

She gave them Bayoumi's guarantor form, triggering an investigation into the man they would come to see as the main facilitator of the two hijackers' lives in San Diego.

Richard Lambert, now retired from the FBI and working as a consultant to the 9/11 families' lawsuit, says "as we began to identify the hijackers' associates, what became clear is that there was a network headed up by Omar al-Bayoumi".

items.title: What tariffs will really cost Canadians and Americans
items.summary: Households and businesses have become used to tariffs impacting the cost of living for more than year now, so what will change now?
items.content:
A raft of new tariffs have been announced during the latest escalation of the trade war between the US and Canada.

The North American neighbours have been locked in a bitter economic conflict since US President Donald Trump launched his flagship trade policy on his return to the White House.

This week saw the latest move by the Canadians with Prime Minister Mark Carney imposing retaliatory import taxes on a host of US goods, after Trump threatened hikes of his own.

As the dust settles in this tit-for-tat tariff row, what will be affected most on both sides of the border?

If Trump's threat to raise tariffs on Canadian vehicles from 25% to 50% from 1 January 2027 becomes a reality, then that would deal a further blow to the automotive industry.

Cars, trucks and parts are among the main goods traded between the US, Canada and Mexico, with the manufacturing sector and supply chains stretching across borders.

Despite previous tariffs increasing costs for manufacturers, car dealerships have absorbed the "lion's share" to date, according to Bernard Yaros, lead economist at Oxford Economics.

"But that cushion is wearing thin," he adds. "The recently threatened 50% tariffs on Canadian autos, trucks, and car parts would feed through to consumer prices more readily than before."

Yaros thinks higher costs on imports to the US could accelerate a trend of manufacturers prioritising luxury cards, SUVs and pick-up trucks and push up prices in the used-car market if supplies of new but less-expensive vehicles becomes tight.

Carney has decided not to match Trump's 50% tariff threat so far, but a 25% import tax on certain American vehicles has been in place since last year.

Construction materials such as steel, aluminium as well as lumber wood have had tariffs in place before the latest escalation, though Canada has now matched US rates on the metals at 50%.

Carney has also imposed import taxes on several US wood products, such as plywood, and even screws used to fix timber together.

That means building firms that import such materials will face higher costs and may choose to pass those on through higher prices - pushing up the cost of homes, for example.

The Forest Products Association of Canada says tariffs would "raise costs on both sides of the border", while on the US side, Bill Owens, chairman of the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB) urged Trump to make building materials exempt from his tariff agenda due to an "ongoing housing affordability crisis".

"Building material tariffs heighten market uncertainty, strain supply chains and increase construction costs," he says.

In 2024 the US imported $23bn (C$32bn, £17bn) worth of wood products, with almost half from Canada, according to a US Congress report.

But the so-called "lumber wars" between the nations on soft wood used in housebuilding are not new and stretch back decades.

Trump says Canada wants 'benefits' of being US state after trade talks collapse

Carney faces crucial test after walking away from Trump's deal

A key factor in this episode of the tariff war is the volume of household items that have been specifically targeted as opposed to raw materials.

Carpets, washing machines, furniture, fridges and even knives, forks and spoons are set to have tariffs applied by Canada.

While there is a risk prices on some of those goods being imported from the US could rise, the more likely scenario is that consumers will turn to domestic alternatives, according to Bradley Saunders, North America economist at Capital Economics.

He says Carney's latest move has intentionally targeted goods where Canadians can "shift to domestic suppliers instead".

"Like hair care products, you really can just buy that domestically instead," he adds.

Saunders explains Carney's response aims to "minimise the impact on Canadian households as much as possible by picking very fungible goods".

The Budget Lab at Yale, which monitors the impact of US government policy on the economy, says it anticipates seeing marginal increases in furnishing and other household equipment for Americans largely due to tariffs on lumber and other materials.

There may not be a material impact on alcohol prices, but it's clear the trade war has had an impact on Canadians' choice of drink.

Many provinces in the country banned US alcohol sales last year in response to previous tariffs, with the American wine and spirits industry saying exports to the country dropped more than 70%.

Carney asked the provinces to restore US alcohol to the shelves during trade talks, but now that they have collapsed, it's likely the ban will return.

Saunders says there's been a big push to "buy Canadian" from politicians and it has been successful when it comes to the strong stuff.

"That's really had an impact on the American alcohol industry," he adds.

Saskatchewan and Alberta are ​the only provinces that still sell ​American alcohol, but the former has announced its own 50% charge on US imported booze, set to kick in on 8 September, when the wider Canadian tariffs do.

While tariffs can end up hitting consumers in the pocket, there are other impacts on households.

Import taxes can complicate trade for businesses that have cross-border supply. As well as the higher costs, the uncertainty created by the trade war could put off investment plans and stunt job creation.

Saunders suggests the biggest impact on households may not just be through prices, but job losses instead.

"If you're, let's say, a bespoke furniture producer in BC [British Columbia], you're now facing a 50% tariff on your exports to the US - that could really shut the business down. I think that would be more the direct impact on households as opposed to these retaliatory measures."

Canada's forest industry employs almost 200,000 people and has called on the government to boost domestic demand through federal housing programs to make greater use of Canadian wood, though it admits "no support package can replace reliable access to our largest export market".

When it comes to US, consumers are unlikely to see much of a difference in terms of the cost of living as result of this latest battle with Canada, but frictions to trade can have longer-term economic impacts.

Such tensions also feed into concerns over the free-trade agreement between Canada, the US and Mexico, known as the USMCA. Both Canada and Mexico have said they want the USMCA extended for another 16 years, but the US has said it will not renew in its current form.

Despite the deal remaining operational, tariffs risk putting off talks in the near future, creating more uncertainty for cross-border trade.

John Iselin, associate director at the Budget Lab at Yale, estimates the cost will only be about $3 per American household on average, but when taking into account Trump's wider trade war with the rest of the world, and particularly China, the added costs rise to about $1,000 for the average family.

"It's hard to view this particular instance with Canada in isolation because we've had similar interactions with a range of other countries, all of which makes doing business harder. It's just another in a series of tariff shocks."

items.title: Canada poaches dozens of top US researchers for its universities
items.summary: Researchers in fields like climate and medicine are being lured north by new research funding.
items.content:
Canada is hiring dozens of researchers from US universities, including top research institutions such as Harvard, as its relationship with its neighbour continues to sour.

More than three-quarters of the 64 professors who are moving to Canada from around the world will come from the US. They will receive funding from a pool of C$504m ($362m; £268m) for research in fields such as climate change and medicine under a new government programme.

US President Donald Trump's administration has accused universities of being dominated by left-wing ideology and diversity policies, and of failing to tackle alleged campus antisemitism.

The BBC contacted the White House and US Department of Education.

The administration has also frozen federal research grants for many different institutions and groups that they have argued were wasteful , external . That uncertainty is helping lure researchers elsewhere.

Meanwhile, Canada is asserting itself more on the global stage while it pushes back against the US in their escalating trade war, which reached a major turning point over tariffs recently .

One climate researcher told the BBC that he was relocating to Canada in part because his work in the US had become more difficult in recent years.

Seth Guikema, a climate resiliency researcher at the University of Michigan and one of the 48 US researchers relocating to Canada, said he had decided to approach Canadian institutions last year in search of opportunities.

"The funding environment in the US for anything related to climate and resilience has become challenging," Guikema said. "I was looking for a good intellectual home where I could have practical impact."

Over the next eight years, Guikema said he would use C$8m to research tools for better preparing for natural hazards, like storms and wildfires, at the University of Western Ontario.

The University of Michigan, his former employer, declined to comment.

Canada's Industry Minister Melanie Joly said on Thursday that the government was "very glad that these fantastic professors are coming".

Asked whether the new government programme was poaching US talent and could be viewed by the Trump administration as an escalation of the US-Canada trade war, she said on Thursday: "The US administration is taking its own decisions and we're taking ours."

Some of the researchers chosen for the programme, like Guikema, were born and raised in the US. Others are Canadians who worked abroad and are now returning home.

Peter Caravan, who for two decades worked as a biopharmaceutical researcher and professor at Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School, appeared emotional at a news conference announcing the research appointments on Thursday.

Caravan is researching how illnesses like cancers and chronic diseases can be better detected - work that will now be done out of the University of British Columbia in Vancouver.

Steven Lamy, a professor of International Relations at the University of Southern California, argued that major grant agencies had "been cut and politicised" by the current US administration.

"All of a sudden employment offers from external universities are attractive," he said.

Stephanie Burt, an English professor at Harvard University, believed the funding cuts were "a generational disaster for science and scientists".

She told the BBC that Canada had offered a "far more welcoming environment" for academics.

US universities are still among the top ranked in the world, according to QS Universities Rankings, with the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), Stanford and Harvard in the top five.

Lynn Pasquerella, the president of the American Association of Colleges and Universities, said institutions felt "helpless" in the face of federal and state cuts.

The deeper concern, she added, was "not the short-term brain drain" but "the possibility that the US could become less attractive as a place to pursue knowledge".

Canada's retaliation tests the limit of American power under Trump

items.title: Boot a Virtual iPhone via Apple's Virtualization.framework
items.summary: Article URL: https://github.com/Lakr233/vphone-cli Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49485267 Points: 365 # Comments: 98
items.content:
Boot a virtual iPhone via Apple's Virtualization.framework using PCC research VM infrastructure.

One command creates a VM end-to-end (download → patch → DFU restore → CFW install → first boot):

vphone-cli vm create runs the whole pipeline; the individual steps below let you drive it manually or re-run one stage.

Update to a newer iOS by pointing fw prepare at an IPSW: --iphone-source /path/to.ipsw --cloudos-source /path/to.ipsw .

Five patch variants with increasing security bypass — pass one to --variant :

See research/0_binary_patch_comparison.md for the per-component breakdown.

Everything vphone-cli creates lives under ~/.vphone/ — kept outside the repo and the .app so the signed bundle stays portable. Redirect the whole tree with $VPHONE_ROOT :

Precedence: the per-item overrides ( $VPHONE_LIBRARY_ROOT , $VPHONE_VENV_DIR ) win over $VPHONE_ROOT , which wins over the ~/.vphone default. The ipsws/ , tools/ , and debs/ caches always sit directly under whichever root is active.

Option A — fully disable SIP, then disable AMFI via boot-arg (most permissive).

Then reboot into macOS and set the AMFI boot-arg (needs SIP fully off to take effect):

Option B — keep SIP on (debug-only relaxed), then allowlist the binary with amfidont (leaves AMFI enabled system-wide).

zsh: killed ./vphone-cli — AMFI/debug restrictions aren't bypassed; see Prerequisites ( amfi_get_out_of_my_way=1 or amfidont ).

Virtualization is not available on this hardware — your Mac is itself a VM; PV=3 guest boot can't nest. Use a non-nested macOS 15+ host.

Stuck on "Press home to continue" — connect via VNC and right-click (two-finger click) to simulate the home button.

System apps won't install — during iOS setup, don't pick Japan or the EU as your region (extra regulatory checks the VM can't satisfy); pick e.g. United States.

App crashes on launch with EXC_GUARD / GUARD_TYPE_MACH_PORT — re-patch with vphone-cli fw patch --variant --force-exc-guard , then re-restore/install ( #291 ). Always on for iOS 18 bases.

Install a .ipa / .tipa — use the running VM's Install menu (drag-drop or file picker).

cfw install hangs re-signing a system binary (e.g. Campo ), memory climbing unbounded — known bug in ldid-procursus up to 2.1.5-procursus7 (the current Homebrew stable ): bytes(uint64_t) calls __builtin_clzll(0) with no zero-guard, which is undefined behavior, and on this build resolves to a 0 -length that underflows an unsigned loop counter — ldid spins writing one byte at a time into a growing buffer instead of terminating. Triggered by any entitlements plist containing an integer value of exactly 0 (some real Apple system binaries have these). Fixed upstream but not yet in a tagged release; rebuild from source: brew install --HEAD ldid-procursus && brew link --overwrite ldid-procursus . Kill the hung ldid process first ( sudo kill -9 ) if you already hit it.

vphone-cli exposes a host control socket ( /vphone.sock ) for programmatic control — screenshots, touch, swipes, hardware keys, clipboard — each action returning an inline screenshot for AI-driven E2E testing. See vphone-mcp for an MCP server wrapping it.

items.title: Guerra in Iran, news. Netanyahu condanna i coloni a Qusra: “Atti criminali di un gruppo ristretto”
items.summary: Araghchi: “Trump sfrutta la guerra per manipolare i prezzi dell’energia”. Pasdaran: “Abbiamo il controllo su Hormuz, gli Usa mentono”. Le Guardie della rivoluzione ribadiscono: “Stretto chiuso a tutte le navi che vogliono transitare senza il nostro coordinamento”
items.content:
"I nostri servizi di intelligence rilevano importanti tentativi di manipolare i mercati dell'energia". Lo ha scritto su X il ministro degli Esteri iraniano Abbas Araghchi , accusando esponenti dell'amministrazione statunitense di sfruttare la guerra per influenzare i prezzi energetici.

I Pasdaran smentiscono gli Stati Uniti e li accusano di mentire. "Il dominio su Hormuz è completamente decisivo – dicono – Lo Stretto rimane chiuso a tutte le navi che intendono transitare senza coordinamento con la Repubblica Islamica dell'Iran". Secondo la nota dei Pasdaran, gli Usa vogliono influenzare il prezzo del petrolio e “coprire i loro fallimenti”.

Stallo dopo sei mesi di guerra. Gli Usa: “Avanti con le sanzioni”

Netanyahu condanna le violenze dei coloni a Qusra. “Arrestarli”

Araghchi: “L’amministrazione Trump sfrutta la guerra per manipolare i prezzi dell’energia”

Araghchi: “Guerra Usa-Israele fallita, da basi Usa no sicurezza”

“Nell'ultima settimana a Hormuz 29 navi al giorno, aumenta il traffico”

Wafa, due morti in attacchi israeliani con droni nella Striscia di Gaza

Due palestinesi sono rimasti uccisi e altri tre feriti in due diversi attacchi con droni, attribuiti alle forze israeliane, avvenuti nella Striscia di Gaza: lo riferisce l’agenzia palestinese Wafa . In un caso, aggiunge la stessa fonte, il raid è avvenuto a Gaza City, con il bilancio di un morto e due feriti. L'altro episodio ha avuto luogo in serata vicino a Khan Yunis: in questo caso si parla di un morto e un ferito. Dal canto suo, l'Idf ha reso noto in serata di aver "eliminato" nella Striscia di Gaza, senza precisare in che aree, un comandante e un cecchino di Hamas, considerandoli individui che "costituivano una minaccia immediata" nella Striscia di Gaza.

Il viceministro degli Esteri iraniano Kazem Gharibabadi ha dichiarato che "l'Iran non ha fretta di riaprire lo Stretto di Hormuz . L'accordo sullo Stretto di Hormuz con l'Oman non entrerà in vigore finché gli Stati Uniti non rispetteranno i loro impegni".

Ghalibaf attacca Bessent sull’impatto della guerra: “Bugiardo”

Il presidente del parlamento iraniano e capo negoziatore Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf ha accusato il segretario al Tesoro statunitense Scott Bessent di aver mentito sull'impatto economico della guerra con l'Iran e del blocco imposto da Washington. "Bugie, bugie, ti stanno bruciando i pantaloni", ha scritto Ghalibaf in un post sul social X, citando un articolo di Bessent secondo cui il blocco e l'Operazione Esclusione Economica avrebbero "schiacciato la già fallimentare economia iraniana" e che gli Stati Uniti avevano guidato l'esportazione di 130 milioni di barili nei 14 giorni precedenti, mentre l'Iran non ne aveva esportato nessuno. "Per i veri 130, dite al vostro collaboratore di consultare i dati di Moody's che mostrano oltre 130 miliardi di dollari di costi di guerra, e chiedete a qualcun altro quanto Jane Street ha bruciato oltre ai 130 milioni di dollari vendendo allo scoperto il petrolio per conto vostro in una sola operazione sui future", ha aggiunto Ghalibaf.

Netanyahu condanna le violenze dei coloni a Qusra. “Arrestarli”

Il premier israeliano Benjamin Netanyahu ha condannato "con fermezza gli atti criminali di violenza" commessi nelle località palestinesi di Qusra e Jalud, in Cisgiordania, da "un gruppo ristretto di rivoltosi". "Stanno violando la legge, causando una grave ingiustizia alla comunità ebraica rispettosa della legge, ostacolando l'esercito nello svolgimento delle sue missioni e danneggiando l'immagine di Israele nel mondo", ha affermato Netanyahu. Il premier ha riferito che le forze di sicurezza sono intervenute rapidamente, hanno sequestrato tre veicoli e posto fine agli incidenti in breve tempo. "L'esercito, lo Shin Bet e la polizia stanno conducendo una rigorosa indagine sul terreno e mi aspetto che le autorità arrestino i rivoltosi e li consegnino alla giustizia il prima possibile", ha concluso.

"Poco fa, l'Idf ha colpito un comandante di Hamas nella zona di Deir al-Balah", nella Striscia di Gaza, "che stava pianificando attentati contro soldati ed era attivo nella riabilitazione delle capacità militari di Hamas, in violazione del cessate il fuoco. L'attacco è stato condotto per eliminare la minaccia". Lo riporta il portavoce dell'Idf in una nota, secondi cui "il terrorista colpito si nascondeva all'interno del complesso dell'ospedale Shuhada Al-Aqsa, in un altro esempio dell'uso cinico delle infrastrutture umanitarie da parte di Hamas per promuovere attività terroristiche". L'agenzia stampa palestinese Wafa riporta l'uccisione di un uomo nell'area di Deir al-Balah poco fa

L'esercito e la Polizia di frontiera israeliani sono intervenuti oggi nella località palestinese di Qusra, a sud di Nablus, nel nord della Cisgiordania occupata, dopo l'arrivo di un gruppo di coloni israeliani e gli scontri scoppiati con i residenti palestinesi. "Rivoltosi israeliani erano entrati nella zona e si erano verificati scontri, durante i quali sono state lanciate pietre contro palestinesi e altri civili", ha riferito l'esercito in una nota. Secondo la ricostruzione dell'Idf, decine di coloni si sono barricati in un'abitazione palestinese dopo gli scontri. Le forze israeliane sono intervenute per allontanarli dalla casa, separare i due gruppi e proteggere i residenti. L'esercito ha riferito di essere a conoscenza del ferimento di diversi palestinesi, tra cui una donna che ha riportato lesioni lievi ed è stata trasferita dal servizio di emergenza israeliano Magen David Adom per ricevere cure mediche. L'agenzia di stampa palestinese Wafa ha invece riferito che decine di coloni, sostenuti dalle forze israeliane, hanno attaccato una casa a Qusra e circondato le persone presenti all'interno, provocando scontri con gli abitanti. Diversi giovani palestinesi sarebbero rimasti intrappolati nell'edificio, mentre i coloni avrebbero anche incendiato alcuni terreni della zona. L'esercito israeliano ha annunciato di avere sequestrato "diversi veicoli" appartenenti ai coloni e sospettati di essere stati utilizzati per raggiungere la località. I mezzi e altri elementi di prova sono stati consegnati alla polizia nell'ambito dell'indagine aperta sull'accaduto. Gli incidenti avvengono mentre, secondo Wafa, prosegue da 21 giorni l'assedio da parte dei coloni a tre abitazioni palestinesi di Qusra

Idf: “Rivoltosi israeliani hanno attaccato palestinesi a Qusra, condanniamo la violenza”

"Forze dell'Idf e della della polizia di frontiera sono state inviate nella zona di Qusra in seguito a segnalazioni di israeliani giunti nell'area e di violenti scontri, tra cui lanci di pietre contro palestinesi e altri civili. Al loro arrivo, le forze hanno identificato decine di rivoltosi israeliani barricati all'interno di un'abitazione palestinese, mentre i residenti si trovavano all'interno". Lo comunica il portavoce dell'Idf in una nota in merito a nuovi scontri oggi nel villaggio palestinese di Qusra, a sud di Nablus, in Cisgiordania. L'Idf riferisce di essere intervenuto per "rimuovere i rivoltosi israeliani dall'abitazione al fine di proteggere i residenti" e di essere a conoscenza di feriti palestinesi, tra cui una donna evacuata dalla Mezzaluna Rossa. "L'Idf condanna fermamente ogni forma di violenza e continua a operare nelle zone di Qusra e Jalud per prevenire ulteriori scontri e ripristinare l'ordine nella zona", aggiunge la nota

Media: “Cloni aggrediscono giornalisti stranieri in Cisgiordania”

Alcuni coloni israeliani hanno aggredito una famiglia palestinese e dei giornalisti stranieri nel villaggio di Jalud, in Cisgiordania. Lo riferisce l'agenzia di stampa Wafa, come riportato da Al Jazeera. L'agenzia ha riportato le dichiarazioni di Bashar al-Qaryouti, un attivista impegnato contro gli insediamenti nella zona a sud di Nablus, il quale ha riferito che i coloni hanno aggredito Mahmoud al-Toubasi, sua moglie e una troupe giornalistica. Il gruppo si trovava con la famiglia nei pressi dell'abitazione da cui quest'ultima era stata costretta a fuggire mesi prima. I coloni hanno distrutto il veicolo della troupe e hanno aggredito fisicamente i presenti, ha aggiunto l'attivista

Araghchi: “L’amministrazione Trump sfrutta la guerra per manipolare i prezzi dell’energia”

"I nostri servizi di intelligence rilevano importanti tentativi di manipolare i mercati dell'energia". Lo ha scritto su X il ministro degli Esteri iraniano Abbas Araghchi, accusando esponenti dell'amministrazione statunitense di sfruttare la guerra per influenzare i prezzi energetici. "Elementi del governo degli Stati Uniti utilizzano media creduloni per influenzare i prezzi a proprio vantaggio personale e mantenere il presidente degli Stati Uniti impantanato in una guerra che sta perdendo", ha affermato Araghchi. Secondo il capo della diplomazia di Teheran, anche "attori allineati a Israele" promuovono il proseguimento della guerra diffondendo valutazioni eccessivamente ottimistiche. "A pagarne il prezzo reale sono i consumatori americani", ha concluso Araghchi

items.title: Guerra Ucraina - Russia, news. Media, Germania annuncerà presto sanzioni separate contro Mosca
items.summary: Raid russo su un deposito di munizioni vicino Kiev: 37 morti nel rogo. Zelensky: “Terribile negligenza immagazzinare esplosivi vicino alla popolazione”. Tusk: “Mosca prepara escalation per l’autunno, conflitto si allarga”
items.content:
Almeno 37 persone sono morte dopo che un drone russo ha colpito un magazzino dove si trovavano droni ed esplosivi vicino Kiev nella tarda serata di venerdì, provocando un vasto incendio ed esplosioni. Zelensky: “No a magazzini vicino alle zone residenziali, terribile negligenza immagazzinare esplosivi vicino alla popolazione”. È in corso l’incontro tra Alexander Lukashenko e Vladimir Putin a Mosca

Intanto la Germania si prepara ad attribuire alla Russia il fallito attacco con un drone esplosivo all'aeroporto di Lipsia e ad annunciare nuove "ampie" sanzioni contro Mosca. Lo riferisce Politico , citando tre funzionari a conoscenza dei piani del governo di Friedrich Merz .

Putin: “Russia e Bielorussia collaborano attivamente sulla scena internazionale”

Media russi: “In corso l'incontro tra Putin e Lukashenko a Mosca”

Zelensky: “Terribile negligenza immagazzinare esplosivi vicino alla popolazione”

Belgio: “Sull’uso degli asset russi la nostra posizione non cambia, i rischi restano”

Sale a 37 il bilancio delle vittime degli attacchi russi nella regione di Kiev

Media: “Berlino pronta ad accusare la Russia per i droni esplosivi a Lipsia”

Zelensky: “No a depositi di munizioni nelle zone residenziali”

Kiev: “Mosca prepara piani per una possibile offensiva su Kiev e Chernihiv”

Diverse esplosioni sono state udite questa sera a Kiev. Secondo i media locali, la capitale ucraina è nuovamente sotto attacco da parte di droni russi Geran-4. Le autorità hanno invitato la popolazione a seguire le indicazioni di sicurezza e a rimanere nei rifugi fino al termine dell'allerta. Al momento non sono disponibili informazioni su eventuali vittime o danni.

Le forze armate russe hanno colpito un'industria a Kiev e obiettivi nel porto di Nikolayev. Lo ha affermato il Ministero della Difesa russo in una nota. "Droni hanno colpito un'impresa di costruzione navale a Kiev, che assemblava e forniva manutenzione a motoscafi controllati a distanza", si legge nella nota. Gli attacchi al porto di Nikolayev hanno preso di mira un terminal di trasbordo marittimo e quattro strutture di stoccaggio contenenti forniture militari per le forze armate ucraine.

All'inizio della prossima settimana il cancelliere tedesco, Friedrich Merz, dovrebbe annunciare sanzioni separate contro Mosca che potrebbero includere l'espulsione di diplomatici, la chiusura della Casa Russa a Berlino e l'invio di nuove armi all'Ucraina. Lo riferiscono fonti ben informate a Politico . Secondo la testata, Berlino intende motivare le sanzioni con i recenti ritrovamenti di droni esplosivi presso l'aeroporto di Lipsia. Fonti governative hanno riferito a Politico che il vero obiettivo della decisione è indebolire Alternative fuer Deutschland in vista delle imminenti elezioni regionali, in quanto il partito nazionalista chiede una normalizzazione dei rapporti con il Cremlino.

Zelensky: “Il bilancio di morti a Bucha potrebbe aggravarsi”

I soccorritori continuano a rimuovere le macerie nel villaggio di Myla, nel distretto di Bucha, nella regione di Kiev, dopo le esplosioni in alcuni magazzini contenenti rifornimenti militari. Al momento si contano almeno 37 vittime, ma il bilancio potrebbe aggravarsi. "Una situazione terribile e una grave negligenza da parte di chi ha immagazzinato esplosivi proprio accanto alle persone. La distruzione - afferma il Presidente ucraino, Volodymyr Zelensky - è stata ingente e, al momento, si contano 37 morti. Il capo della comunità è stato ucciso mentre partecipava alle operazioni di soccorso. Le mie condoglianze a tutte le famiglie delle vittime. Le operazioni di rimozione delle macerie sono ancora in corso e, purtroppo, il bilancio delle vittime potrebbe aumentare", ha dichiarato Zelensky.

Lukashenko: “Con Putin per fare un bilancio dei risultati, non per prendere decisioni”

Il presidente bielorusso Alexander Lukashenko ha dichiarato, durante i colloqui con Vladimir Putin , che oggi sarebbe stata una giornata dedicata al riepilogo dei risultati, non all'adozione di nuove decisioni. Lo riporta Ria Novosti . "Credo che oggi sarà una giornata dedicata a riassumere alcuni risultati, piuttosto che a prendere decisioni", ha affermato Lukashenko durante l'incontro, dopo aver osservato che i due governi stanno collaborando bene e che non ci sono questioni da risolvere tra Mosca e Minsk, sottolineando che tutti gli accordi vengono attuati.

Putin: “Russia e Bielorussia collaborano attivamente sulla scena internazionale”

Russia e Bielorussia continuano a collaborare attivamente sulla scena internazionale e a rafforzare lo Stato dell'Unione tra i due Paesi. Lo ha dichiarato il presidente russo Vladimir Putin durante il suo incontro con il leader bielorusso Alexander Lukashenko. "Continuiamo a collaborare attivamente sulla scena internazionale e a rafforzare lo Stato dell'Unione", ha affermato citato dalla Tass. Putin ha osservato che il Consiglio dei Ministri dello Stato dell'Unione si riunirà a breve. Inoltre, ha menzionato l'impegno attivo di Mosca e Minsk in tutte le piattaforme internazionali, tra cui le Nazioni Unite, la Csi e l'Organizzazione per la Cooperazione di Shanghai (Sco). "Tutto ciò, ovviamente, sarà anche al centro della nostra attenzione oggi", ha aggiunto

Putin: “Spiegare la guerra ai bambini con la catena alimentare”

Vladimir Putin ha suggerito agli insegnanti di usare la metafora della catena alimentare tra orche assassine e orsi polari per spiegare ai bambini i motivi che hanno spinto la Russia a lanciare l'invasione dell'Ucraina. La questione è emersa durante un incontro tra il leader del Cremlino e gli insegnanti in occasione della Giornata della Conoscenza alla vigilia della ripresa dell'anno scolastico. Dmitry Balanchukov, un insegnante della regione di Belgorod, stava parlando del suo viaggio al Polo Nord. Putin gli ha chiesto se avesse visto orsi polari laggiù. Poi, improvvisamente, ha dichiarato che "le orche assassine mangiano gli orsi come fossero pesciolini", attaccandoli in branco. Putin ha poi sostenuto che vale la pena parlare ai bambini di questi processi che avvengono in natura "per capire in che mondo viviamo" e "perchè stiamo conducendo l'operazione militare speciale"

Mosca: “Nessun motivo per migliorare i rapporti con gli attuali leader della Ue”

Mosca non vede al momento alcun presupposto per un miglioramento delle relazioni tra Russia e Unione europea e accusa gli attuali leader europei di perseguire una linea di confronto nei confronti della Federazione russa. Lo ha dichiarato il portavoce del Cremlino, Dmitry Peskov, come riporta la Tass. "Per ora non vedo alcun motivo per sperare in un miglioramento delle nostre relazioni con l'Europa. Gli attuali politici, l'attuale generazione di politici al potere, sono orientati al confronto, e non solo a parole, ma anche nei fatti", ha affermato Peskov. Secondo il portavoce del presidente russo, i Paesi europei starebbero "mobilitando pienamente le proprie capacità militari e dirigendole contro il nostro Paese, partecipando direttamente alle operazioni militari contro di noi". "Dobbiamo esserne consapevoli. Dobbiamo naturalmente restare aperti alla costruzione di relazioni e manteniamo effettivamente questa apertura, ma dobbiamo anche comprendere perfettamente con chi abbiamo a che fare", ha aggiunto Peskov

Il premier ucraino: “Negligenza criminale per la strage nel distretto di Bucha, i responsabili saranno puniti”

Il premier ucraino Serhiy Koretskyi denuncia "negligenza criminale" che ha portato all'esplosione di un deposito di munizioni nel distretto di Bucha, a seguito di un attacco di un drone russo, con 37 morti e 42 feriti. Koretskyi ha citato l'episodio analogo avvenuto a Vyshneve, sempre nella regione di Kiev, lo scorso sei luglio, deplorando che "non è servito da lezione. Nel quinto anno di guerra, commettere gli stessi errori è negligenza criminale. I responsabili, senza eccezioni, dovranno essere puniti seriamente", ha dichiarato. A Vyshneve erano rimaste uccise, nelle esplosioni di un deposito di munizioni, nove persone. Più di 280 abitazioni avevano subito danni

Media russi: “In corso l'incontro tra Putin e Lukashenko a Mosca”

Il presidente russo Vladimir Putin sta incontrando il suo omologo bielorusso Alexander Lukashenko nella sua residenza nella regione di Mosca, Novo-Ogaryovo. Lo riporta Interfax. Il leader bielorusso è arrivato in Russia giovedì per una visita di lavoro, e ieri ha avuto colloqui con il primo ministro russo Mikhail Mishustin. Il consigliere presidenziale russo Yury Ushakov aveva precedentemente affermato che la visita di Lukashenko in Russia non era ufficiale e che i due leader avrebbero parlato informalmente dopo il loro incontro

Zelensky: “Terribile negligenza immagazzinare esplosivi vicino alla popolazione”

Belgio: “Sull’uso degli asset russi la nostra posizione non cambia, i rischi restano”

"Il Belgio ha sempre sostenuto che gli asset russi debbano rimanere congelati finché la Russia non cesserà la sua guerra di aggressione contro l'Ucraina e non risarcirà quest'ultima per i danni causati. La questione del loro utilizzo è del tutto diversa. Su questo punto, la posizione belga è ben nota e coerente. Non è cambiata dall'anno scorso". Lo afferma un portavoce del ministro degli Esteri belga Maxime Prévot interpellato dall'ANSA, precisando che "i rischi associati al loro utilizzo non sono magicamente scomparsi" e che "Prévot ribadirà questa posizione ai suoi omologhi europei nella riunione Gymnich dell'1 e 2 settembre"

items.title: Berlin is being blackmailed by hackers, mayor says
items.summary: Kai Wegner says the German capital and city-state would not cave in to a ransom demand for data stolen in a cyber-attack.
items.content:
Berlin is being blackmailed by hackers who were able to compromise city systems and steal data earlier this month, its mayor has said.

Kai Wegner said officials would not cave in to the ransom demand, which came on Thursday evening. He did not say how much was being sought, though Der Spiegel reports the hackers are demanding 30 bitcoin, worth around €2m (£1.7m).

Some of the German capital's online systems were forced to close down as a result of the attack, while investigators were working to understand what data had been taken.

The Rhysida group, which is thought to operate from Russia and eastern Europe, and was behind a previous attack on the British Museum, has reportedly taken responsibility.

It has said on its website it intends to begin auctioning the 5.79 terabytes of data it was able to steal from Berlin in seven days' time, according to news agency Reuters.

He said state police, prosecutors and federal security services were working to investigate the suspected perpetrators "with the utmost urgency", adding that inquiries into the "content and scope of the compromised data are being pursued with great intensity".

Officials for the city-state said an initial data leak occurred between 7 and 12 August.

Then, on 14 August, two department networks were shut down, making applications for housing benefits and payments impossible for several days.

Forensic investigations had since revealed further data leaks within Berlin's transport and environment department, officials said.

"It cannot be ruled out that personal or other non-public data may also be affected," the mayor's office said in a statement on Friday.

Authorities in the capital have not named the suspected cyber-attackers, though Der Spiegel is carrying a screenshot of the Rhysida group's dark web site claiming to possess files including contracts, non-disclosure agreements, personnel files, passwords and thousands of personal contact details.

It is also displaying a countdown, after which it says it will begin auctioning off the data with a starting price of 30 bitcoin - the same amount of the cryptocurrency being sought from Berlin, the German newspaper reports.

The Rhysida group has claimed hundreds of attacks since it emerged in 2023, studies say, and the group has targeted government insititutions and businesses of varying sizes in numerous countries.

It successfully infiltrated the British Museum's computer systems in 2023, disrupting services and stealing around 500,000 files.

When the UK institution refused to pay the ransom, the group published the files - containing the personal data of visitors, subscribers and staff - on the dark web.

The Berlin cyber-attack comes roughly a month before the city holds elections, though state senator Iris Spranger insisted that election infrastructure had not been compromised.

items.title: 97-year-old woman rescued after Nepali floods looked like 'a warrior'
items.summary: A 97-year-old woman, Guna Maya Bohara, survived the flash floods and was rescued using an excavator.
items.content:
A 97-year-old woman pulled from flood debris in Nepal is recovering in hospital, according to her doctors.

Guna Maya Bohara's great-nephew, Dipak Bohara, has told BBC Nepali she looked like "a warrior" who had returned victorious from battle.

The operation to pull Bohara out of the rubble of her care home took four hours.

Bohara travelled from Kathmandu to help rescue his great-aunt.

Hundreds of people have been confirmed dead after Wednesday's flash floods, which scientists believe were triggered by a glacier collapsing in the Himalayan border region with Tibet.

Video produced by Mansi Kapur and Kamal Pariyar. Video edited by Suneth Perera, Jasmin Dyer and Andrew Webb.

items.title: Greenland says findings on genocide allegation not final
items.summary: Experts examined the use of forced contraception on the Inuit community during the 1960s and 70s.
items.content:
Greenland's justice minister has said the government cannot conclude whether genocide was committed against the Inuit community after experts examined the use of forced contraception in the 1960s and 70s.

"We cannot say, on behalf of the government, whether there was genocide," Marianne Paviasen told reporters. "This is something we can continue to debate."

Two reports on the practice were released on Friday, a year after Denmark apologised for the treatment of Inuit women and girls in its autonomous territory.

Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said a "reconciliation commission" would be set up while Danish PM Mette Frederiksen promised the governments would work together.

Denmark has passed a compensation law to pay 300,000 Danish crowns (£34,404; $46,800) to each woman affected by the policy.

Records from the national archives show that, between 1966 and 1970, 4,500 Greenlandic women and girls, some as young as 13, had an intra-uterine device (IUD) implanted under a birth-control programme administered by Danish doctors.

In recent years, many women came forward to say they had been fitted with an IUD without their knowledge or consent.

Use of the birth control was so widespread that Greenland's population growth severely slowed.

Frederiksen issued an apology last August to Greenlandic women and their families affected by "systematic discrimination".

In 2024, a former prime minister of Greenland, Mute B Egede, described the practice as "genocide".

Under the UN Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide , external , one definition of genocide is "imposing measures intended to prevent births" within a "national, ethnical, racial or religious group".

The territory tasked a panel of four experts with establishing whether human rights had been violated and whether such violations met the definition of genocide.

However, the panel split, with two members resigning and producing a separate report.

The two experts who remained, Alaskan lawyer Dalee Sambo Dorough and University of Copenhagen law professor Miriam Cullen, found in their report that the rights of Inuit women in Greenland had been violated.

But they said that they could not conclude that genocide had taken place "on the basis of contraceptive practices alone".

They added that genocidal intent by Denmark remained a "possible inference" that a court might establish, based on evidence that fell outside the scope of their report, such as the removal of Inuit children to be raised by Danish families.

The rival report, produced by Jonas Christoffersen, former head of the Danish Institute for Human Rights, and Jensine Nedergaard, a psychologist who had worked in Greenland, accepted that women had been wronged but could not establish the extent of their mistreatment.

They found no evidence "any authority or health professional at any time had any intention of destroying the Greenlandic population".

Reacting on Friday, Greenland's justice minister said the two reports were so different that one "says there was no genocide at all" while the other "says there could have been".

Greenland contraception scandal victims hear Danish PM's emotional apology

Denmark apologises to Greenland's forced contraception victims

One woman affected by the forced contraception policy, Henriette Berthelsen, told news agency AFP before the reports were presented that their conclusions had been skewed from the start because no Greenlandic Inuits had been appointed as experts.

"For me, this is not just about history or politics. It's my body, my life and my right to self-determination," she said.

"And once again, I see that it is others who will investigate and define what was done to me and to other Inuit women."

Another woman, Inger Platou, 70, told Reuters that she remembered waking up from what she had been told was a minor operation to discover an IUD had been inserted without her consent.

"It turns out we were treated like animals," she said. "Without consent, they just wanted to stop women from giving birth or having children. It was a very inhumane act."

A doctor, she added, later told her complications from the coil had left her unable to become pregnant. She went on to adopt two children from Colombia.

"We are very deferential to authority because we are colonial children," she said.

Reacting to the reports on Friday, Frederiksen said: "We will handle the political process together with the government of Greenland. The most important thing for me is that we find the right path together."

Greenland was a Danish colony until 1953 and did not gain home rule until 1979. Copenhagen continued to oversee its healthcare system until 1992.

The Inuit, or mixed Danish and Inuit, make up nearly 90% of the island's population of 56,000.

The birth-control campaign was designed to control the territory's population, which had ballooned since the 1950s, aided by modernisation and better healthcare. This growth, in addition to an increasing rate of teenage pregnancies, had alarmed the Danish authorities.

In 1970, the campaign was considered a "success" as fertility rates had fallen sharply, though the rate continued to fall for some time after that. In the eight years from the campaign's inception in 1966 until 1974 when it levelled off, Greenland's fertility rate plunged from seven children per woman to 2.3.

items.title: US plans to cut off military aid to key Middle East ally, BBC told
items.summary: Iraqi Kurdistan fears the Trump administration's plan will make the region more vulnerable to further attacks from Iran.
items.content:
The Trump administration is planning to cut off military aid to a key Middle East ally that helped the US defeat the Islamic State group (IS) and is now facing punishing attacks from Iran, according to four sources familiar with the matter.

The US Department of Defense has told leaders of Iraq's semi-autonomous Kurdistan region in recent meetings that the administration is not planning to renew an expiring agreement that provides security assistance to the Peshmerga, the Kurdish security force.

The BBC spoke to two officials who participated in the talks and two other sources with direct knowledge of the issue. The sources spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe the talks, details of which have not been previously reported.

Kurdish officials fear the funding cut would create a power vacuum and embolden Iran, which has fired hundreds of missiles and drones into Iraqi Kurdistan since US President Donald Trump started the war with Tehran.

Ending the Peshmerga's security assistance would undermine a longtime partner in Iraq, analysts said, and send the message that the US cannot be trusted to back its allies in the region.

"The US would be cutting off the Kurds, who shed so much blood to help the Americans achieve their goals in Iraq and the wider Middle East," Yerevan Saeed, the director of the Global Kurdish Initiative for Peace at American University, said.

"This is going to be a big win for Iran, China, and Russia if the Kurds are left so exposed."

In his second term, Trump has pledged to reduce America's foreign entanglements in regions like the Middle East. He also launched the war with Iran, which reached the six-month mark on Friday with no end in sight.

The memorandum of understanding between the Pentagon and the Kurdish Regional Government (KRG) is set to expire on 30 September, the same day the US and other nations are withdrawing their last remaining troops from Iraq.

The troop withdrawal will formally end the international military campaign against IS, in which the Peshmerga fought alongside coalition troops to end the jihadist group's control of parts of Iraq and Syria. The sole remaining US military base in the country, located in the Iraqi Kurdish capital of Irbil, is set to close next month once coalition troops leave.

The Peshmerga, which has approximately 180,000 troops in Iraqi Kurdistan, received $61m (£45m) in the fiscal year 2026 for weapons, military training and stipends through the Pentagon's counter-IS programme.

The Pentagon proposed cutting all the group's security aid in its fiscal year 2027 budget request - arguing that since IS was defeated the money should now be reallocated - but the spending plan is on hold amid a broader budget battle in Congress.

The request raised alarm bells in Iraqi Kurdistan, but officials had held out hope that the US would renew the funding through an extension of the current deal.

The fears have only grown as Iran has stepped up attacks against the KRG. Iran and Iranian-backed militias had conducted 158 missile or drone attacks inside Iraqi Kurdistan by late May, according to reasearch on the latest available data compiled by the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a Washington DC think tank.

But despite the surge in attacks, in recent talks with Iraqi and Kurdish leaders, defence department officials said the US was not planning to extend the memorandum of understanding, multiple sources with knowledge of the discussions said. The Pentagon signed the initial memorandum of understanding giving military assistance to the Peshmerga in 2016 and renewed it in 2022.

A final decision on security engagement between the US and Kurdistan is still being reviewed, according to one source familiar with the Pentagon's thinking. The US is considering ways to maintain some security support in both Iraq and Iraqi Kurdistan after the troop withdrawal, the sources said.

The KRG declined to comment. The White House referred the BBC to the Pentagon where a spokesperson pointed to a statement by the department summarising Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth's meeting with Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi in July.

"The United States, Iraq and Coalition partners have achieved tremendous success in defeating ISIS and now the Iraqi Security Forces, including the Peshmerga and other Iraqi Kurdistan Region security forces, will lead the fight against terrorists in Iraq," the statement said.

A State Department spokesperson told the BBC it was focused on implementing the troop withdrawal, and "ensuring that Prime Minister Zaidi is positioned to disarm Iran-aligned terrorist militias and safeguard Iraqi sovereignty."

The expiration of the security aid for the Peshmerga would come less than one year after the US opened its largest consulate in the world, in Irbil.

At the ribbon-cutting ceremony for the $800m complex last December, Michael Rigas, a senior US State Department official, said the consulate was "a testament to the value of the relationship between the United States and the Iraqi Kurdistan Region".

The recent discussions around Kurdish security were part of larger conversations between the US, the Iraqi government and KRG over the upcoming troop withdrawal. That date was set under a 2024 agreement between Washington and Baghdad to withdraw the US troops that remain in Iraq from the campaign against IS. American combat troops left Iraq in 2011 but returned after the power vacuum led to the rise of IS in 2014.

The US could avoid repeating the same mistake by continuing to back the Peshmerga, said James Jeffrey, who spearheaded the global coalition against IS in Trump's first term.

"It's money well spent, as we found out when the Islamic State rolled into northern Iraq," said Jeffrey, a former US ambassador to Iraq and Turkey under the Obama administration.

The Trump administration has not said how many US troops brought in to fight IS more than a decade ago remain in Iraq. Experts believe it's under 1,000, down from 170,000 at the height of the Iraq War.

The recent meetings on Iraqi security included the White House, Defense and State Departments, with Tom Barrack acting as a principal US voice on Iraq, four sources said. A close Trump ally, Barrack is the US ambassador to Turkey and special envoy to Iraq and Syria.

The administration has said publicly it's open to a bilateral security agreement with Iraq. The countries discussed a possible defence pact in the recent meetings, but it's still unclear how the agreement might be structured or what Iraqi Kurdistan's role might be.

Al-Zaidi touted the troop withdrawal during his visit to Washington last month. Al-Zaidi, who was elected in May, met Trump at the White House, as well as Hegseth and members of Congress.

"October 1 will mark a new day in the trajectory of the Iraqi state, as Iraq will be free of any foreign military presence," al-Zaidi's office said in a statement at the time.

The withdrawal will reduce the exposure of US troops in the Middle East who have been targeted by Iran during the war, analysts said. Tehran has attacked US bases across the region, including the base in Irbil.

But it will leave the Peshmerga security force and the rest of the region it helps protect even more vulnerable than before, said Jason Campbell, a former US defence official.

"The Peshmerga have been the frontline in the US and international war with ISIS," said Campbell, an expert at the Middle East Institute. "If the US moves forward with this, it'll make the Kurds perhaps the most vulnerable potential targets of Iran."

Under drone fire, exiled Kurds wait to confront Iranian regime

items.title: Russia ramps up rhetoric but wants to avoid war with Nato, Western officials say
items.summary: But they say Moscow will likely continue its "hybrid activity" against Nato members, short of direct military action.
items.content:
Russian President Vladimir Putin wants to avoid a direct military confrontation with Nato, despite increasingly hostile rhetoric aimed at the UK and other allies over their support for Ukraine, Western officials believe.

Some reports have suggested the visit by CIA chief John Radcliffe to Moscow this week was, in part, to warn Russia against a possible attack on a member of the Euro-Atlantic military alliance.

But the Western officials, who asked not to be named, said recent warnings from Moscow, including that UK forces could be targeted in future or that its weapons factories could be hit, were "nothing new".

They were, they suggested, consistent with Russia's military doctrine to apply pressure on the West.

The officials suggested that the hostile rhetoric was also a reflection of the growing pressure Putin is facing at home, with slow and costly gains in Ukraine along with the impact of Ukrainian long-range strikes deep inside Russia.

Putin and his officials have repeatedly dismissed warnings of Russian plans to attack Nato countries as hysteria. And US President Donald Trump appears to believe the Russian leader – saying this week that "he's not going to attack a Nato territory".

Not long before launching his full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Putin had given public assurances that he had no intention of attacking Russia's neighbour - despite overwhelming US intelligence that such preparations were in full swing.

However, the senior Western officials said on Friday that Russia would likely continue its "hybrid activity", short of direct military action, using methods such as cyber-attacks, sabotage and even assassination attempts.

They said that was aimed at breaking Western resolve and support for Ukraine. One official highlighted the risks of that Russian strategy leading to a miscalculation -which could spark a military confrontation.

Russia is suspected of being behind a string of recent drone incidents in several Nato countries.

Earlier this month, a drone loaded with explosives reached a runway in Germany's Leipzig airport - a key logistics hub for transferring military equipment to Ukraine. There is no proof to link the incident directly to Russia, which has denied any role.

It came amid a string of drone sightings over European airports and military bases that began last year and which are also suspected of being the work of Russia, though it again denies this.

Following the Leipzig incident, the head of France's security services warned that "we must consider the possibility of direct, more violent hostile actions on our national soil".

Still, one Western official said Nato allies should remain calm but not complacent. The UK government has already made clear that recent Russian threats will not deter its support for Ukraine.

The Western officials said the Ukraine war had "escalated" this year, with both Moscow and Kyiv stepping up their own long-range strike campaigns.

Putin, they said, had not changed his maximalist objectives, despite some signs of increasing frustrations back home.

They said petrol shortages in Russia were having an impact on support for the war. They believed there was increasing political pressure on the Russian leader, but that this did not pose a critical challenge to his power.

Russia is still making slow gains in the eastern Donbas region. But it's also facing heavy casualties.

The officials said Russia was losing 6,000 more soldiers a month - either killed or wounded - than it can recruit.

That said, there is no indication yet that the Kremlin leader will resort to mass mobilisation.
